intro: Notre-Dame-du-Chêne, Viroflay's parish church, took its name from an oak: one already centuries old at the edge of the Forêt de Meudon when the church went up in 1966. A 2009 tape measure, 527 centimetres round, puts it somewhere between 450 and 550 years old. Through the cholera epidemics of the 1850s and 1870s people walked out to pray beside it and left ex-votos in its bark, and some still do. Free to reach, on a road verge, no gate. A second champion tree stands a short train ride away in La Celle-Saint-Cloud.
meta_description: The Chene de la Vierge: a 450-550 year old pilgrimage oak in Viroflay, France, beside the Foret de Meudon, plus a second champion tree nearby.
question_meta: Viroflay's remarkable tree is the Chene de la Vierge, a centuries-old pilgrimage oak at the edge of the Foret de Meudon.
question_answer: Viroflay's notable tree is the Chene de la Vierge, a Pedunculate Oak roughly 450 to 550 years old standing alone at the edge of the Foret de Meudon. It carries the label Arbre remarquable de France and has been a pilgrimage site, an arbre a clous, since the cholera epidemics of the 1850s and 1870s.
question_context: The oak stands alone on the verge of the Route du Pave-de-Meudon, where the Foret de Meudon gives way to the road, and it gave its name to the church built nearby in 1966, Notre-Dame-du-Chene, rather than the other way round. Its age is derived rather than counted: a 2009 measurement put the girth at 527 centimetres, and a published growth rate for a slow oak gives a range of 450 to 550 years. Through the Paris region's cholera epidemics of the 1850s and 1870s, people walked out to pray and left objects in its bark, which is how it earned the names arbre a clous and arbre a loques; ex-votos are still attached today. France's Arbres remarquables register listed it in 2002. A short train ride away in La Celle-Saint-Cloud, a multisecular sweet chestnut stands as the centrepiece of a square redesigned to show it off; it won France's national Tree of the Year vote in 2021 and placed eighth at the European final in 2022.

faq.q: What is the remarkable tree in Viroflay?
faq.a: The Chene de la Vierge, a Pedunculate Oak roughly 450 to 550 years old standing alone at the edge of the Foret de Meudon.
Yes. It stands on the open verge of a departmental road with no gate or entry restriction.

faq.q: Why is it called the Chene de la Vierge?
faq.a: During the cholera epidemics of the 1850s and 1870s, people came to pray beside it and left ex-votos in its bark, a devotional practice that gave it the names arbre a clous and arbre a loques and continues today.

faq.q: Is the chestnut tree actually in Viroflay?
faq.a: No. The Multisecular Chestnut of Audran Square stands in La Celle-Saint-Cloud, a separate town about 5.5km away, five minutes' walk from its own train station. From Viroflay it is one change of train at Saint-Cloud; from central Paris it is a direct ride on Transilien line L.

trees.story:
The church is named after the tree, not the other way round. Notre-Dame-du-Chêne was built in 1966 and took its name from an oak that had been standing at the edge of the Forêt de Meudon for centuries before anyone laid its foundation stone. The same tree sits on Viroflay's coat of arms.

Nobody has counted its rings. What exists is a tape measure: 527 centimetres round when it was last recorded in 2009, a trunk 1.68 metres through, which at the rate a slow oak puts on wood works out at somewhere between 450 and 550 years. The sixteenth century, roughly, and the range is as tight as the method honestly allows.

Its second life began with cholera. Through the epidemics that went through the Paris region in the 1850s and 1870s, people walked out here to ask for help and left something behind, which is how it became an arbre à clous and an arbre à loques, a nail tree and a rag tree. Ex-votos still hang on it, and it is still used as an open-air place of worship. A hundred and fifty years of visitors, for a reason that has nothing to do with its girth.

France's Arbres remarquables register added it in 2002, and the national forestry office has since had its health formally assessed. Thirty metres tall, alone on a road verge, out of the wood it once belonged to.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ex-votos left on its bark and by the trunk, 527 centimetres round. It stands alone on the verge of the Route du Pavé-de-Meudon, out in the open where the Forêt de Meudon ends.
trees.access: Free. Stands isolated beside a busy departmental road at the edge of the Forêt de Meudon, a public pilgrimage and walking site with no gate or entry restriction.
trees.transport: Viroflay Rive Gauche station (Transilien), about 600m, roughly a 10-12 minute walk.

location.address: Place du Général Audran, La Celle-Saint-Cloud, Yvelines (not Viroflay)

trees.access: Free. Stands as 'the central piece of a square, redeveloped especially to showcase' it (contest page's own wording), Place du Général Audran, a public town square in the La Chataigneraie residential quarter of La Celle-Saint-Cloud. No gate, ticket or restriction mentioned in any of three independent sources.
trees.transport: DAY-TRIP ADDITION, genuinely in La Celle-Saint-Cloud, NOT Viroflay: the tree stands about 295m (a 4-5 minute walk) from Gare de La Celle-Saint-Cloud (Place Jean Mermoz), which is a direct stop on Transilien Line L, about 20-25 minutes from Paris Saint-Lazare with no change. From Viroflay (Rive Droite or Rive Gauche stations), also on Transilien lines through Saint-Cloud, the honest journey is one change at Saint-Cloud onto the La Celle-Saint-Cloud-bound branch of Line L; total journey is roughly 25-30 minutes door to door depending on the timetable, not a direct line. State this as a same-network day trip with one change, never as walking distance from Viroflay.
trees.story:
This chestnut's shape was cut into it by winegrowers. Its branches used to be lopped to make stakes for the vineyards, which is why it grew low, wide and twisted rather than tall, with bark that spirals up the trunk and a crown now eighteen metres across.

It was once a lonely tree in the middle of a meadow. Then the town grew all around it, and La Celle-Saint-Cloud did something towns rarely do for a tree that is in the way: it redesigned a square, Place du Général Audran, specifically to show it off. The chestnut is the centrepiece, in a residential quarter called La Châtaigneraie, the chestnut grove.

The European contest page, French Wikipedia and a Paris news site all give it about 330 years, and Le Parisien reported in 2022 that it went in under Louis XIV. That is an estimate repeated consistently, not a ring count, and nobody has published its girth. If you have measured it, tell us.

In 2021 it was voted Île-de-France's tree of the year, then won France's national public vote, nominated by the heritage-tree association A.R.B.R.E.S. At the European final in 2022 it placed eighth of sixteen, with 28,119 votes.

It does not stand in Viroflay. It stands in La Celle-Saint-Cloud, a five-minute walk from the station, direct on Transilien line L from Paris Saint-Lazare; from Viroflay the trip takes a change at Saint-Cloud.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, wide, twisted crown, about 18 metres across, and the bark spiralling up its trunk. It stands as the centrepiece of Place du Général Audran, five minutes' walk from La Celle-Saint-Cloud station.

best_time.label: October, when the chestnuts ripen in their spiny burs
